item.title: Weiss v. Maine Soapstone Co.
item.description:
STATE OF MAINE APPELLATE DIVISION WORKERS’ COMPENSATION BOARD Case No. App. Div. 26-0002 Decision No. 26-10
JEROME WEISS (Appellant)
v.
MAINE SOAPSTONE COMPANY , INC. (Appellee)
and
MAINE EMPLOYERS’ MUTUAL INSURANCE COMPANY (Insurer)
Decided: October 8, 2026 Conference held: September 2, 2026
PANEL MEMBERS: Administrative Law Judges Biddings, Chabot, and Rooks By: Administrative Law Judge Biddings [¶1] Jerome Weiss appeals from a decision of a Workers’ Compensation Board administrative law judge ( Smith, ALJ) denying his Petition to Reopen for Mistake of Fact or Fraud. Mr. Weiss contends that the ALJ erred in determining that his petition was untimely under 39-A M.R.S.A. § 321(2), and in concluding that even if the petition had been timely, Mr. Weiss did not establish that Maine Soapstone Company committed fraud. We disagree with Mr. Weiss’s contentions and affirm the decision.
2
I. BACKGROUND1 [¶2] Mr. Weiss sustained a work-related shoulder injury on February 3, 2009, while working for Maine Soapstone Company. Initially, Maine Soapstone voluntarily paid Mr. Weiss lost time and medical benefits. On September 13, 2010, Maine Soapstone issued a 21-day letter informing Mr. Weiss and the board of their intention to discontinue Mr. Weiss’s benefits as of October 5, 2010. See 39-A M.R.S.A. § 205(9). [¶3] In response to the discontinuance of his benefits, Mr. Weiss filed a Petition for Review , Request for Provisional Order , and a Petition for Award of Compensation regarding the February 3, 2009, date of injury. During the litigation, Mr. Weiss underwent an independent medical examination with Dr. Hall. See 39-A M.R.S.A. § 312. Dr. Hall opined that the effects of Mr. Weiss’s injury were ongoing and that he had retained a partial work capacity. An evidentiary hearing was held on May 16, 2011, before a board hearing officer (Pelletier, HO).2

item.title: Authentication of certified electronic records or data
item.description:
STATE OF MAINE SUPREME JUDICIAL COURT AMENDMENT TO MAINE RULES OF EVIDENCE
2026 Me. Rules 04
Effective: November 1, 2026
All of the Justices concurring therein, the following amendment to the Maine Rules of Evidence is adopted to be effective on the date indicated above. The specific amendment is stated below. To aid in the understanding of the amendment, an Advisory Note appears after the text of the amendment. The Advisory Note states the reason for recommending the amendment, but the Advisory Note is not part of the amendment adopted by the Court.
1. Rule 902 of the Maine Rules of Evidence is amended to read as follows:
RULE 902. EVIDENCE THAT IS SELF-AUTHENTICATING
The following items of evidence are self -authenticating; they require no extrinsic evidence of authenticity in order to be admitted:
. . . .
(13) Certified Records Generated by an Electronic Process or System. A record generated by an electronic process or system that produces an accurate result, as shown by a certification of a qualified person that complies with the certification requirements of Rule 902(11) or (12). The proponent must also meet the notice requirements of Rule 902(11).
(14) Certified Data Copied from an Electronic Device, Storage Medium, or File. Data copied from an electronic device, storage medium, or file, if authenticated by a process of digital identification, as shown by a certification of a qualified person that complies with the certification requirements of Rule 902(11) or (12). The proponent also must meet the notice requirements of Rule 902(11).
2 Advisory Note – November 2026
Subdivision (13) has been added to provide a procedure by which parties can authenticate certain electronic evidence other than through the testimony of a foundation witness. On March 30, 2026, the Media Bureau of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) issued a “public no- tice” about the FCC’s lowest unit charge (LUC) require- ments. Those requirements, which are outlined in 47 U. S. C. §315(b)(1)(A), concern favorable rates that broad- casters must charge for campaign advertisements in the weeks leading up to elections. The notice stated that polit- ical candidates, joint fundraising committees with noncan- didate members, and political parties engaged in coordi- nated political activity are entitled to the LUC. Four candidates for Congress filed an application for re- view with the FCC, arguing that only political candidates are entitled to the LUC and asking the full Commission to set aside the public notice as unlawful. Two months later, while their application was still pending before the Com- mission, the candidates filed a petition for review against
2 FCC v. BROWN Per Curiam the FCC and the United States in the Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit seeking the same relief. A divided panel of the Fourth Circuit determined that it had jurisdiction to consider the candidates’ challenge, granted their petition, and set aside the public notice. In doing so, the majority reasoned that the plain text and legislative history of §315(b)(1)(A) limits the availability of the LUC to political candidates. item.title: Consent judgment orders California-based home appliance company to pay $800K to 339 employees denied overtime pay
item.description: LOS ANGELES – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment requiring a home appliance company to pay $800,000 in back wages and damages to 339 employees after an investigation found the company violated federal wage laws.The judgment comes after the department’s Wage and Hour Division investigated Coway USA Inc. and found that the employer paid employees on a piece-rate basis and failed to pay employees for time spent attending mandatory meetings, picking up and loading supplies, and performing work before and after their shifts, in violation of the Fair Labor Standards Act. Investigators also found that Coway did not include nondiscretionary incentives, bonuses, and commissions in overtime pay calculations and frequently reduced the number of hours employees recorded working on their timecards.Entered in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on Sept. 9, the consent judgment requires Coway to record all hours the implicated employees worked, including time they spend picking up supplies, attending mandatory training, and communicating with customers before and after appointments. Coway is also required to give employees pay statements that show their hours worked, services provided to customers, and the rate Coway paid for the hours and services. The consent judgment orders Coway USA Inc. to pay $400,000 in unpaid overtime wages and an equal amount in damages to 339 employees working in the greater metro areas of Los Angeles, New York City, and Washington, D.C. The company also agreed to pay $10,000 in penalties for willful violations. Coway USA Inc. is a subsidiary of Coway Co. Ltd., a multinational company specializing in home appliances. The company installs and maintains various appliances, including water and air filtration products throughout the U.S.Employers and employees can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). item.title: US Department of Labor announces field assistance bulletin withdrawing 3 opinion letters on tipped employees
item.description: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced the issuance of a new field assistance bulletin addressing the treatment of related duties performed by tipped employees under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Field Assistance Bulletin No. 2026-1 brings the division’s guidance on tipped employees with dual jobs into alignment with current regulations.The bulletin withdraws the division’s 1979, 1980, and 1985 opinion letters concerning the application of dual jobs regulations to tipped employees. The withdrawal of the three opinion letters is necessary because they no longer reflect the division’s policy or interpretation of the FLSA. The bulletin also clarifies that the current dual jobs regulation focuses on whether an employee performs duties related to the employee’s tipped occupation, rather than imposing a specific percentage-based limit on the time an employee may spend performing related, non-tipped duties within that occupation.The publication of the new bulletin follows a 2024 federal court decision that vacated the department’s 2021 dual jobs final rule. After that decision, the department removed the regulatory text adopted under the 2021 rule and reinstated the original dual jobs regulations.The new field assistance bulletin clarifies that no current Wage and Hour Division guidance relies on the former percentage-based limit on the time a tipped employee may spend performing related, non-tipped duties, commonly known as the 80/20 rule. item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced the issuance of a new field assistance bulletin addressing the treatment of related duties performed by tipped employees under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Field Assistance Bulletin No. 2026-1 brings the division’s guidance on tipped employees with dual jobs into alignment with current regulations.The bulletin withdraws the division’s 1979, 1980, and 1985 opinion letters concerning the application of dual jobs regulations to tipped employees. The withdrawal of the three opinion letters is necessary because they no longer reflect the division’s policy or interpretation of the FLSA. The bulletin also clarifies that the current dual jobs regulation focuses on whether an employee performs duties related to the employee’s tipped occupation, rather than imposing a specific percentage-based limit on the time an employee may spend performing related, non-tipped duties within that occupation.The publication of the new bulletin follows a 2024 federal court decision that vacated the department’s 2021 dual jobs final rule. After that decision, the department removed the regulatory text adopted under the 2021 rule and reinstated the original dual jobs regulations.The new field assistance bulletin clarifies that no current Wage and Hour Division guidance relies on the former percentage-based limit on the time a tipped employee may spend performing related, non-tipped duties, commonly known as the 80/20 rule. The division removed its 80/20 rule guidance from its Field Operations Handbook in January 2025, and the handbook is now consistent with the reinstated 1967 dual jobs regulations.As noted in the most recent regulatory agenda, the department is developing a notice of proposed rulemaking to amend various regulations for tipped employees under the FLSA. The department welcomes public comments on the proposed rule once it is published.Learn more about the Wage and Hour Division, including the agency’s enforcement of tip regulations under the FLSA.Read Field Assistance Bulletin No. 2026-1.
